items.title: A free multi-CDN, jsDelivr style
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
The experiment lives at cdn.jamesst.one, which now serves a copy of this site, and you can watch where it is routing at rum.jamesst.one.

The above diagram is actually a simplification, because before that, a client first has to look up the IP address to connect to, i.e. DNS. A multi-CDN hooks into the DNS reply and picks which CDN is best, then that CDN’s anycast picks which specific data center based on network routing rules.

The CDN is chosen in DNS. When your resolver asks for cdn.jamesst.one, the answer is a CNAME to one of three CDNs, and which one depends on where you are. Or, more accurately, the network you are on.

The first version used a small script on the page that read Resource Timing entries and beaconed them home. Which works but I would rather not put JS on pages for this. jsDelivr itself gets its RUM data from elsewhere: I think it used Cedexis, then PerfOps, rather than running a script of its own.

items.title: Let's Play with Hardcaml!
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
I prepared a five-minute lightning talk for the 8th Homebrew CPU Meetup on November 28, 2026. The slides are below.

Open slides in a new tab · Download PDF · View Markdown source

This talk is a gentle introduction to Hardcaml, an RTL design library embedded in OCaml. Rather than discussing advanced verification techniques, I wanted to share the fun of building digital circuits in an interactive programming environment.

We start with a simple 5-bit counter and do everything inside utop, an OCaml REPL:

No FPGA, external Verilog simulator, or even a separate OCaml project is needed to try this example. I tested the installation steps and the REPL session in a Docker environment, so you can follow along with the slides.

With the help of AI coding agents, I ended up building a dual-core RISC-V SoC that boots Linux 6.18 with SMP on a Colorlight i9 FPGA board.

I hope this talk encourages more people to give Hardcaml a try and enjoy building their own digital circuits.

I'm working on a recursive algorithm using ColdFusion custom tags and I ran into a strange bug. It seems that in Adobe ColdFusion 2025 (update 14 at the time of this writing), if you use attributeCollection to "spread" a struct into a custom tag with no other data attributes, any changes made to the attributes scope internally to the custom tag get applied directly to the passed-in struct. This means that mutations to the attributes scope can leak into the calling context.

items.title: Will The “Big Web” Kill RSS?
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
Recently, I noticed my favourite Reddit feeds were no longer working in my RSS reader app. I assumed an outage of some sort, but the cause was more sinister. Reddit has deliberately removed access via RSS.

Because RSS is now a common surface for large-scale scraping and automated abuse, we'll stop supporting RSS feeds on November 13, 2026 while preserving moderation workflows that depend on it through supported alternatives. Read full announcement

So it’s doing this under the pretext of preventing AI scrapers from helping themselves to its content, but forgive me for being cynical. For a long time now, Reddit has been reducing options for readers, beginning a few years back with an attack on 3rd party apps such as the beloved Apollo , and now forcing visitors to use their own (enshittified) app.

Notes:

Fun! It's would be hard for me not to like a book that covers both lexicography and the Battle of the Wilderness.

It's a stark example of a book written right before it was obvious how big the Internet was going to be. I also wanted a lot more algorithmic detail than I got about how exactly Dr. Minor's research system was more efficient than the OED status quo.

I don't know how fair this is, but I also found myself thinking it was a very pre-generative-AI book. items.title: Going by; Laughing; Living.
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Do you hear all this noise? It's frightening.

The sky is pink, and orange, and yellow all washed-out by the grey of the clouds.

A group of people is going by, they are laughing, they are living.

And I wonder how.

I'm trying to understand, how can I go by? How can I laugh? How can I live?

Why aren't they walking alone?

The room is getting dark, the colors have faded.

I can't hear the people anymore, but they are still walking around my brain.

They are going by, they are laughing, they are living.

Getting my head through the window, I am looking at the trees. Looking right in their eyes.

"I'm sorry", I tell them.

You didn't deserve this.

"You are precious", I tell them.

And I wonder why I don't hear it coming from everywhere.

Why is there only this scary noise?

The noise of life going on, of people going by.

As if it was all ok. As if all around us wasn't screaming.

But the noise is too loud, too loud to listen with our ears.

In this article I’ll share the results of ad-hoc security vulnerabilities research I’ve done on windows 8 apps deployment. Specifically, we’ll discuss fundamental design flaws that allow to Reverse Engineer Win8 apps, modification of installed apps and the negative implications on Intellectual Property rights protection, Licensing models and overall PC security. Finally we’ll discuss some creative ideas on how to mitigate these security issues. 

 

Meet the mother-load: C:\Program Files\Applications

All Windows 8 applications in the developer preview are installed under the clandestine C:\Program Files\Applications location. I will hazard a guess and say that once the Windows App Store goes online it will install all apps under that folder. Currently the folder is an invisible one and cannot be accessed from Windows Explorer user interface on a new Win8 developer preview install.

items.title: Help me choose my new MacBook - durable screen edition!

items.excerpt:
What's the lightest and most durable MacBook? The screen on my 2020 MacBook Air was unacceptably fragile. Black Friday means I'm replacing it tomorrow, and this time I want one that's durable!

I've owned maybe 8 Mac laptops in my life, and I'm hard on them: I lug them in a backpack and drop them a few times a year. But I've never broken the screen... until now, because my 2020 Macbook Air screen is broken in three places!

Both bottom screen corners cracked after separate instances of sliding off the bed and falling just 2 feet onto a rug! The screen is so thin that these gentle impacts dented the metal corners and cracked the glass. It also shuts with no clearance - I accidentally half-closed it with a squishy foam earplug (!) resting in the hinge, and this very small and soft item cracked the plastic screen bezel and the underlying glass.

Now the whole screen flickers, has lines, and retains ghost images, to the point where I can't read comfortably. But my old MacBooks withstood…

You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.
